newsitem.title: USA: US airline security seen hinging on national will.
newsitem.headline: US airline security seen hinging on national will.

text.p: A U.S. Congressional aviation specialist said on Monday he hoped new recommendations to improve aviation security will not meet the same fate of those made after the bombing of Pan American Flight 103 in 1988.

Rep. James Oberstar, a Minnesota Democrat and former chairman of the House aviation subcommittee, asked: "Do we have the national will to stand up for the long haul for the cost and inconvenience of aviation security?"
President Clinton formed a special commission after the midair explosion of Trans World Airlines Flight 800 off New York's Long Island on July 17. The crash killed all 230 people on board.
Investigators at first thought a bomb caused the blast, but no conclusive evidence has been found, and they now are said to be leaning toward blaming an explosion in one of its fuel tanks.

Oberstar told an aviation security conference sponsored by the King Publishing Group that recommendations made after the Flght 103 bombing over Scotland included screening luggage and background checks of airport workers.
But many of the recommendations were rejected amid concerns about the cost, he said.
Citing the World Trade Center bombing in New York, Oberstar said terrorism was not just a foreign phenomenon. "We need a changed attitude about domestic security," he said.
The TWA commission has made preliminary recommendations to improve passenger and baggage screening, to improve airport security and to increase the use of bomb-sniffing dogs.
Oberstar said funding for security was a national issue and should not borne by airlines but by general taxes.
"This is a shared responsibility, not a unique responsibiity of air carriers," he said. "The target is not the symbol of any our U.S. carriers. It is the U.S. flag."

National Transportation Safety Board Chairman James Hall, a member of the TWA commission, said the panel was on the right track, including its regulations to have the board coordinate the handling of next of kin of aviation victims.
Families of victims have often complained about callous treatment from the airline-owner of the crashed plane.

Discussing the Flight 800, Hall said his agency would continue to dredge the ocean bottom to try to bring up more parts of the downed plane and to start to build a three dimensional mock-up of it from parts already brought up.
He also said a contract had been given the California Institute of Technology to determine the explosive characteristics of the jet fuel in the plane.
"We intend to work very closely with the FBI and other authorities until we are convinced that we have pursued every possible credible scenario," Hall said.
